chapter_theme: A song at Kavalur (காவளூர்): the poet describes lovemaking with women versed in Kama's arts and asks to escape the ruin of that delusion and reach Murugan; the praise tells Rama's war for Sita and the slaying of Vali.

882.reading: The poet describes deer-eyed women with milk-sweet speech and pearl-strung breasts, bangles crying as they make love, shame dropped and garments loosened, reciting the texts of Kama, and asks whether, escaping the ruin of that delusion, he will reach Murugan. The praise names Rama who, in anger at Janaki's captivity, destroyed Lanka, gave Sugriva the kingdom and Tara and felled Vali with an arrow, as uncle, the lover of the kura girl who kept watch on the platform in the hunters' millet field, and the lord at Kavalur of areca groves where the three Tamils are known.
882.nuance: வேளின் நூல்களைக் கற்ற விளம்பவும்: the women recite Kama's texts, love as a learned art. ஆகும் மோக விபத்து: the delusion is called a calamity. The headword is printed காவ்ளுர் and the last line reads காவளூர்.

links.note: 882 has the women recite the texts of Kama (வேளின் நூல்களை கற்ற விளம்பவும்) as they make love, and calls the delusion a calamity (மோக விபத்து). 370, at Arunai, has the women's carp eyes speak the scripture of Rati's lord (ரதிபதி சுருதி மொழிவன). In both songs love is given a learned text, the god Kama's scripture, so that the seduction is presented as an art taught and recited, not a passing impulse.

source_issues: Heading of chapter 181 reads காவ்ளுர்; song 882 names the place காவளூர் (line 24).
